newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Red chip Beijing Enterprises set to smash records.
newsitem.headline: Red chip Beijing Enterprises set to smash records.

text.p: Beijing Enterprises Holdings Ltd's share issue is set to smash stock market records this week, feeding off a red-chip craze blazing through Hong Kong in the run-up to Chinese rule, analysts said.
"A lot of Chinese people say this is a gift from the (Chinese) government before the handover," said Ricky Tam, senior research manager at Delta Asia Securities.

The red-chip conglomerate launched its initial public offering (IPO) last Tuesday and generated massive demand from Hong Kong investors. Red chips are Hong Kong-incorporated firms with financial backing from the mainland.
Thousands of people queued for hours to get application forms for the offering and scrambled to hand them in before Friday's noon deadline.
Sources close to the underwriters said the Hong Kong offering was more than 1,000 times subscribed, a record, and tied up about HK$200 billion in the Hong Kong banking system.
"People are borrowing from banks, from their friends," said Alex Tang, head of research at Yamaichi International.
"The chances of getting shares are slim," he added.
GITIC Enterprises Ltd holds the current subscription record. The company, also a red chip, launched an initial public offering in March which was 892 times subscribed.
Beijing Enterprises, controlled by the Beijing municipal government, is due to make its market debut on Thursday, May 29.
The company offered 150 million shares globally at HK$12.48 per share. Ten percent was offered to the public in Hong Kong and 90 percent was offered to international investors.
Analysts said the stock could more than triple in value on its first day of trade, with the grey market price quoted at HK$38-39 on Friday.
"For sure, it will have a strong debut," said Michael Ng, analyst at ASG Investment.
Investors expect the Beijing municipal government to inject valuable assets into Beijing Enterprises at attractive prices, boosting the company's share price.
The conglomerate already owns a stake in Beijing McDonald's, the company that operates the fast-food chain in the city. It also has interests in brewing, toll roads, hotels and retailing.
The stock is expected to follow in the footsteps of red-chip favourite Shanghai Industrial Holdings Ltd
Shanghai Industrial, controlled by the Shanghai municipal government, launched an IPO at HK$7.28 per share last May. It has since risen more than fivefold, closing at HK$44.00 on Friday.
"Due to the past experience with Shanghai Industrial, investors hope Beijing Enterprises may repeat the story," said Ann Shih, head of China research at Kleinwort Benson Securities.

But some analysts said huge gains could trigger strong profit-taking and the stock's short-term upside may be limited, with the grey market price pointing to a price earnings multiple (P/E) of more than 60 times compared with an issue price P/E of 19 times.
"Strong profit-taking is expected. Such a handsome capital gain would even make institutions join in the profit-taking," said one analyst.
Beijing Enterprises has forecast a net profit of not less than HK$350 million for the year ending December 1997.
Analysts said the company could reap HK$200 million in interest income from subscription monies.
